html: Reinforced Decision Intelligence Lab Reliable reinforcement learning and learning-based control with mathematical guarantees for autonomous and industrial systems. Donghwan Lee, Associate Professor · School of Electrical Engineering · KAIST Learn more about our research through videos on our [lab’s YouTube channel] Research Identity How can learning systems make effective decisions while remaining stable, robust, and safe? Our lab develops reinforcement-learning and decision-making methods grounded in control theory, optimization, and applied mathematics. We study fundamental theory and translate it into algorithms for robotics, autonomous driving, energy, and industrial systems. Three Research Pillars Foundations of Reinforcement LearningWe establish convergence, finite-time, and sample-complexity guarantees for Q-learning, temporal-difference learning, and related algorithms, including function approximation, distributed learning, and Markov games. Safe and Robust Learning-Based ControlWe design learning-based controllers that account for disturbances, model uncertainty, unsafe exploration, and stability requirements, with particular interest in Lyapunov and control-theoretic methods. Autonomous and Industrial IntelligenceWe collaborate on robotics, autonomous driving, GPU power management, and industrial process control, connecting theoretical insight with deployable systems. title: Research
html: Research Our central question is: How can an agent learn from data while preserving stability, robustness, safety, and efficiency? We connect reinforcement learning with control theory, optimization, stochastic approximation, and machine learning. This combination allows us to develop new algorithms, explain why they work, and adapt them to autonomous and industrial systems. Three Research Pillars Foundations of Reinforcement LearningWe study the mathematical foundations of sequential decision making. Our work develops convergence and finite-time analyses for Q-learning, temporal-difference learning, value iteration, and policy-evaluation methods. We are particularly interested in function approximation, target networks, experience replay, distributed learning, multi-agent games, and alternative Bellman operators. Representative topics: switching-system models of Q-learning; finite-time and sample-complexity analysis; stable learning with function approximation; regularized and target-based algorithms; distributed and game-theoretic reinforcement learning. We develop reinforcement-learning and control methods that explicitly account for these requirements. Control-theoretic tools provide both algorithmic structure and mathematical certificates. Representative topics: robust policy gradients; disturbance attenuation; minimax reinforcement learning; Lyapunov-based analysis; safe exploration; stability and convergence certificates; learning-based control of dynamical systems. Representative topics: robotics and autonomous systems; vision-language decision making; SLAM reliability; offline reinforcement learning; industrial process control; energy and computing systems. title: Collaboration
html: Collaboration Projects & Collaboration We build collaborations around clearly defined technical problems. Our goal is to connect rigorous reinforcement-learning and control methods with platforms, data, and operational needs from academic, public-sector, and industrial partners. What We Contribute Algorithm Development Reinforcement learning, offline RL, robust RL, safe learning, multi-agent learning, and learning-based control. Theory and Certification Convergence, finite-time analysis, stability, robustness, Lyapunov methods, and control-theoretic interpretation. Simulation and Evaluation Problem formulation, benchmark design, simulation environments, baselines, ablation studies, and quantitative evaluation. Algorithm Integration Adaptation to robotics, autonomous driving, industrial processes, energy systems, and computing infrastructure. Collaboration Areas Autonomous-driving perception, reasoning, and control Industrial AI, process control, energy, and computing systems Reliable reinforcement-learning algorithms and theory Multi-agent decision making and coordination Vision-language models for sequential decision making Engagement Models Robotics, drones, and autonomous systems Joint government-funded research proposals Industry-sponsored research and technical validation Algorithm development for an existing platform or dataset Independent evaluation, benchmarking, and theoretical analysis Education & Training We provide lectures, seminars, short courses, and customized training programs in reinforcement learning and signal processing for universities, research institutes, companies, and public organizations. Courses can cover topics ranging from fundamental concepts to advanced mathematical theory and practical implementation, including deep reinforcement learning, safe and robust learning, digital signal processing, estimation, filtering, and data-driven signal analysis. The content and format can be tailored to the participants’ backgrounds and application needs. Start a Conversation For a focused initial discussion, please send a short description of the problem, the available platform or data, the expected outcome, and the intended project structure. title: Presentations
html: Presentations Research talks and paper explainers from the Next State AI YouTube channel. Each presentation includes a short overview and links to the paper and video. [video] Browse the paper presentation playlist Donghwan Lee, Han-Dong Lim, "A Switching System Theory of Q-Learning with Linear Function Approximation," [arxiv] [video] [project] Models Q-learning with linear function approximation as a stochastic switching linear system. The joint spectral radius provides finite-time error bounds and convergence certificates that can be less conservative than bounds based on a single update. [video] Donghwan Lee, "Spectral Analysis of Heavy-Ball Q-value Iteration," [arxiv] [video] [project] Studies when heavy-ball momentum can accelerate Q-value iteration. An exact switching-system representation connects convergence to the joint spectral radius and gives conditions under which the momentum method is faster than standard Q-value iteration. [video] Donghwan Lee, "Sign-Separated Asymmetric Finite-Time Error Analysis of Q-Learning," [arxiv] [video] [project] Separates Q-learning errors into positive and negative components to study overestimation bias. Distinct finite-time upper bounds reveal how maximization affects the two components differently; the rate separation concerns the bounds and need not occur along every sample path. [video] Donghwan Lee, "Switching Theory for Q-Learning," [arxiv] [video] [project] Develops a switching-system analysis of tabular Q-learning with a constant step size. It expresses finite-time convergence rates through the joint spectral radius and connects this quantity to deterministic-policy modes and a linear-programming characterization. [video] Donghwan Lee, "Beyond the Bellman Fixed Point: Geometry and Fast Policy Identification in Value Iteration," [arxiv] [video] [project] Explains how value iteration can identify an optimal greedy policy before its value estimates reach the Bellman fixed point. A geometric switching-system analysis separates policy identification from value convergence and gives conditions for faster convergence in the policy-relevant directions. [video] Donghwan Lee, Hyukjun Yang, "Bellman Residual Minimization for Control: Geometry, Stationarity, and Convergence," NeurIPS 2026 [arxiv] [conference] [video] [project] Investigates hard and soft Bellman residual objectives for control, connecting their geometry, stationary points, and descent methods. The analysis distinguishes tabular optimality and convergence guarantees from stationarity under function approximation, and examines smoothing bias and policy recovery. [video] Narim Jeong, Donghwan Lee*, "Finite-Time Analysis of Minimax Q-Learning," RLC 2025, RLJ 2025 [journal] [video] Derives finite-time error bounds for minimax Q-learning and its smoothed variant in discounted two-player zero-sum games. Upper and lower comparison systems separate the effects of initialization, constant-step sampling noise, and smoothing under the stated tabular sampling assumptions. [video] Han-Dong Lim, Donghwan Lee*, "Finite-Time Analysis of Temporal Difference Learning with Experience Replay," Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2024 [arxiv] [journal] [video] [project] Quantifies how experience replay affects temporal-difference learning under Markovian observations. Finite-time bounds for averaged and final iterates show how replay-buffer capacity and mini-batch size control the error associated with a constant step size. [video] Han-Dong Lim, Donghwan Lee*, "Backstepping Temporal Difference Learning," ICLR 2023, Kigali, Rwanda, May 1-5, 2023 [arxiv] [conference] [video] [project] Uses backstepping from nonlinear control to understand and design stable off-policy temporal-difference algorithms with linear function approximation. The framework unifies existing methods and motivates a new convergent algorithm, illustrated on problems where standard TD learning can diverge. [video] Han-Dong Lim, Donghwan Lee*, "Regularized Q-Learning," NeurIPS 2024 [arxiv] [conference] [video] [project] Adds a suitable regularization term to stabilize Q-learning with linear function approximation. Switching-system analysis establishes convergence and bounds the error of the resulting solution, clarifying the tradeoff between stability and regularization bias. [video] Donghwan Lee, "Final Iteration Convergence Bound of Q-Learning: Switching System Approach," IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control, vol. 69, no. 7, 2024 [arxiv] [journal] [video] [project] Establishes a finite-time error bound for the final Q-learning iterate using a discrete-time switching-system model. The result analyzes the estimate directly used by the algorithm, without requiring an additional average of past iterates. [video] Donghwan Lee, Jianghai Hu, and Niao He, "A Discrete-Time Switching System Analysis of Q-Learning," SIAM Journal on Control and Optimization, vol. 61, no. 3, 2023 [arxiv] [journal] [video] [project] Represents asynchronous Q-learning with a constant step size as a stochastic affine switching system. Upper and lower comparison dynamics yield finite-time error bounds and help explain the role of overestimation in learning. [video] Donghwan Lee, Han-Dong Lim, Jihoon Park, and Okyong Choi, "New Versions of Gradient Temporal-Difference Learning," IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control, vol. 68, no. 8, 2023 [arxiv] [journal] [video] [project] Introduces variants of gradient temporal-difference learning through a common convex-concave saddle-point formulation. This viewpoint connects off-policy learning with primal-dual dynamics, supports stability analysis, and enables a systematic comparison of the proposed algorithms. [video] Donghwan Lee, "Convergence of Dynamic Programming on the Semidefinite Cone for Discrete-Time Infinite-Horizon LQR," IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control, vol. 67, no. 10, 2022 [arxiv] [journal] [video] [project] Analyzes dynamic programming for the discrete-time infinite-horizon linear quadratic regulator using matrix inequalities and norm bounds. It establishes convergence of Q-value iteration under the stated initialization conditions and extends the analysis to policy iteration with exponential convergence guarantees. [video] Donghwan Lee and Niao He, "A Unified Switching System Perspective and Convergence Analysis of Q-Learning Algorithms," NeurIPS 2020 [arxiv] [conference] [video] [project] Provides a common convergence framework for Q-learning algorithms by expressing their associated differential equations as switched linear systems. The approach covers asynchronous and averaging Q-learning and gives a sufficient convergence condition for Q-learning with linear function approximation. [video] Donghwan Lee and Niao He, "Periodic Q-Learning," L4DC 2020, Online, June 10–11, 2020 [arxiv] [conference] [video] [project] Studies tabular Q-learning with separate online and periodically refreshed target estimates. Holding the target fixed connects the inner updates to stochastic optimization, enabling finite-time analysis and sample-complexity guarantees for finding a near-optimal policy. [video] Donghwan Lee and Niao He, "Target-Based Temporal-Difference Learning," ICML 2019, Long Beach, CA, June 11-15, 2019 [arxiv] [conference] [video] [project] Develops temporal-difference algorithms that maintain separate online and target parameters. Averaging, double, and periodic target updates receive convergence analyses, including finite-sample results for periodic TD, providing a theoretical perspective on target networks in linear policy evaluation. [video]

title: Video Lectures
html: Video Lectures Next State AI · Lecture Series 1 Reinforcement Learning Explore the mathematical foundations of reinforcement learning through definitions, step-by-step derivations, proofs, and worked examples. This series follows Donghwan Lee’s Reinforcement Learning: Mathematical Foundations and Algorithmic Principles, connecting the book’s concepts with the algorithms they support. [video] Watch the lecture series [video] Start with Lecture 1 About the book The companion textbook builds the mathematical framework for sequential decision-making, from Markov decision processes and value functions to Bellman equations, dynamic programming, and learning from sampled experience. Read the relevant sections alongside the videos to follow the notation, revisit the proofs, and work through the examples. Donghwan LeeGauss Press · First edition, 2026 View the book on AmazonBrowse our books Topics covered Markov decision processes: states, actions, transitions, policies, rewards, and discounted returns. Value functions and Bellman equations: state and action values, advantage functions, contraction mappings, and optimality. Dynamic programming: value iteration, stopping rules, linear programming, and occupancy measures. Mathematical tools: gradient methods, regression, entropy, KL divergence, and softmax. Learning from experience: stochastic approximation, Monte Carlo prediction, and exploration. Begin with Lecture 1 on MDPs, transitions, and policies, then follow the playlist in order. Each video description identifies the corresponding book sections and pages and provides chapter timestamps for review. For the full lecture collection and research videos, visit the Next State AI YouTube channel.

title: PI
html: Principal Investigator Biography -Donghwan Lee Donghwan Lee is an Associate Professor in the School of Electrical Engineering at KAIST and an adjunct faculty member in the KAIST Robotics Program. His research develops reliable reinforcement-learning and learning-based control methods with mathematical guarantees, with applications to autonomous and industrial systems. He received a B.S. in Electrical Engineering from Konkuk University, an M.S. in Electrical Engineering from Yonsei University, and an M.S. in Mathematics and a Ph.D. in Electrical and Computer Engineering from Purdue University. From 2017 to 2020, he was a postdoctoral researcher in the Coordinated Science Laboratory at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.
